taxonomy.title: Vascular — carotid and cerebrovascular disease
taxonomy.scopeIn: Carotid symptoms, imaging, medical/operative/endovascular selection, perioperative neurologic events and relevant cerebrovascular anatomy.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Traumatic cerebrovascular injury belongs to trauma-head-spine-extremities. Nonvascular neurologic essentials belong to neuro-orthopedic-essentials.
taxonomy.priorityReason: A focused symptom-attribution and intervention lane can move beyond a few stenosis rules.
taxonomy.coverageReason: At most four distinct live clinical concept identities cover this scope. Variants repeat those identities.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

scopeBoundaries.scopeIn: Head injury, GCS, spinal injury, traumatic cerebrovascular injury, pelvic ring stabilization, limb trauma and compartment/vascular assessment.
scopeBoundaries.scopeOut: Nontraumatic nerve localization belongs to neuro-orthopedic-essentials. Pelvic visceral injury and global survey belong to trauma-initial-abdomen. Generic reversal biology belongs to hematology-transfusion-coagulation.

scopeBoundaries.scopeIn: Nontraumatic peripheral nerve localization, postoperative nerve injury outside a specific operative-family objective, musculoskeletal mimics and urgent orthopedic infection essentials.
scopeBoundaries.scopeOut: Traumatic head/spine/extremity care belongs to trauma-head-spine-extremities. Hernia-specific pain belongs to hernia-groin. Thyroid laryngeal injury stays in thyroid-nodules-cancer.

independentPassReferences.title: Bilateral carotid treatment priority
fairness: The observed eye-covering sequence localizes the event to the right eye despite the tighter left stenosis. Combining that attribution with the recent transient event and supplied operative context supports early right endarterectomy.

Both side and timing components occur equally across the four options; there is no convergence, uniquely qualified key or key-only word match. The left-sided greater stenosis is a credible clinical lure.
Two steps: localize the visual event, then prioritize symptomatic disease and timing rather than the numerically tighter lesion.
Importance: high for vascular surgery and resident examination content. Realism: credible vascular-clinic decision with nondisabling symptoms and operative context.

'Early' and 'deferred' are qualitative, not an operational scheduling order. The item supports relative priority; it does not independently verify an exact timing interval or procedural risk standard.
suggestions: Retain the balanced four-option matrix and eye-specific observations.

During clinician review, confirm that the qualitative timing contrast is sufficient for the intended objective. If actual scheduling is tested later, use source-supported explicit time windows in a new reviewed version.

answerChoices.label: Right endarterectomy with early scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: The cover-eye history localizes the transient deficit to the right eye. The recent symptomatic right lesion has priority despite the larger asymptomatic measurement on the left.

answerChoices.label: Left endarterectomy with early scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the larger numerical stenosis as the symptomatic target despite the event localization.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This treats the larger numerical stenosis as the symptomatic target despite the event localization.

answerChoices.label: Right endarterectomy with deferred scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: The current lack of recurrent symptoms does not erase the significance of the recent symptomatic severe lesion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The current lack of recurrent symptoms does not erase the significance of the recent symptomatic severe lesion.

answerChoices.label: Left endarterectomy with deferred scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: This both assigns the wrong side to the event and defers the symptomatic-lesion assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This both assigns the wrong side to the event and defers the symptomatic-lesion assessment.

questionVariant.explanation: Covering the unaffected eye left the impaired right eye in use; covering the right eye restored vision through the left. The right carotid lesion is therefore the recent symptomatic severe lesion. Prompt endarterectomy assessment together with medical therapy is appropriate for this represented operative context; the opposite side's larger percentage does not establish symptom causation. The four side/timing combinations are balanced rather than allowing majority-component assembly.

decisionNodes.stem: Which revascularization priority best fits {patientName}'s event and completed evaluation?

answerChoices.label: Right endarterectomy with early scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: The cover-eye history localizes the transient deficit to the right eye. The recent symptomatic right lesion has priority despite the larger asymptomatic measurement on the left.

answerChoices.label: Left endarterectomy with early scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: This treats the larger numerical stenosis as the symptomatic target despite the event localization.

answerChoices.label: Right endarterectomy with deferred scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: The current lack of recurrent symptoms does not erase the significance of the recent symptomatic severe lesion.

answerChoices.label: Left endarterectomy with deferred scheduling
answerChoices.rationale: This both assigns the wrong side to the event and defers the symptomatic-lesion assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: Covering the unaffected eye left the impaired right eye in use; covering the right eye restored vision through the left. The right carotid lesion is therefore the recent symptomatic severe lesion. Prompt endarterectomy assessment together with medical therapy is appropriate for this represented operative context; the opposite side's larger percentage does not establish symptom causation. The four side/timing combinations are balanced rather than allowing majority-component assembly.

reasons: The fourth CTA key is a cosmetic eye/age substitution with no distinct consequential objective.
A current renal trajectory now changes the vascular modality decision. This materially expands the original CTA objective and receives a separate concept version with previousConceptId.
Remove the task phrase that interpreted the kidney findings for the learner.
The fourth management version repeats the same supplied eligibility and implausible delay/medication-stop alternatives.
Use age, function, recovered renal trajectory and operative anatomy to compare CEA with a credible transfemoral option.
Preserve the established severe-symptomatic-CEA meaning; later context explicitly updates the earlier renal problem.
Another identical CTA selection adds little breadth.
Replace future supply with expert-reviewed discordance across the intervention threshold and a specific acquisition limitation.
New meaning: selective invasive resolution. Keep the old definition and FSRS history intact.
Repeated prompt-CEA selection has no independent discriminator.
Replace with interpreting the normal-distal versus bulb denominator before deciding whether revascularization is supported.
Different clinical meaning gets a new concept ID, not reassigned prompt-CEA history.
The old task tests a supplied severe-lesion confirmation rule with weak brain-MRI/echo competitors.
A second expert duplex can corroborate severity; categorically dismissing it is misleading. The revision distinguishes missing arch/intracranial mapping from a second severity measurement.
Keep the established confirmatory-imaging concept and remove treatment-answer scaffolding from first-node feedback.
One-year review, stopping prevention and waiting for another event are caricature competitors.
Supply actual function, infarct and neck observations and compare early CEA, early transfemoral CAS and infarct-related deferral.
Keep the established CEA-selection identity and exact older history.
The third confirmation rule duplicates existing supply.
Replace with the conflict between severe symptomatic narrowing and a large disabling infarct.
New management objective is a named-patient outside-hospital chart review in clinic.
The third management task repeats supplied suitability and weak alternatives.
Replace with a later recovery assessment where serial adequate imaging shows persistent cervical occlusion with collateral distal filling.
Prior feedback addresses timing, not the later occlusion/bypass decision.
Exact review-two PASS and manager acceptance bind the full case; preserve it.
Eye-cover observations require localization before prioritizing the symptomatic side over the tighter opposite lesion. The balanced side/timing matrix resists convergence.
Qualitative timing and the given operative context are accepted limitations. No clinical approval or exact scheduling cutoff is inferred.
This retained predecessor is superseded by supported independently passed v2.
Its original priority wording and surveillance competitor are less resistant to preinterpreted localization.
Propose excluding v1 from future supply in favor of exact existing v2; create no extra draft and preserve both histories.

questions.stem: Which left carotid treatment plan follows from Jonah Price's completed measurements?

exhibit.caption: Constructed measurement record; fictional values, not a copied clinical image

answerChoices.label: Continue medical prevention and carotid follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The NASCET reduction is 1 - 3/5 = 40%, below the ordinary symptomatic CEA threshold.

answerChoices.label: Arrange left carotid endarterectomy with medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Using the estimated bulb gives the outside 70% figure but does not yield a NASCET 70% lesion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Using the estimated bulb gives the outside 70% figure but does not yield a NASCET 70% lesion.

answerChoices.label: Arrange left carotid stenting with medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: A less invasive procedure does not create a revascularization indication for ordinary sub-50% disease.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A less invasive procedure does not create a revascularization indication for ordinary sub-50% disease.

questions.explanation: NASCET uses the normal distal ICA: 1 - 3.0/5.0 = 40%. The estimated bulb produces a different measurement, 1 - 3.0/10.0 = 70%. Apply the symptomatic treatment evidence to the NASCET result: routine CEA or CAS is not the plan for this mild lesion. Continue prevention and follow-up.

questions.stem: Which long-term left carotid plan best fits Nora Lewis's current vascular findings?

answerChoices.label: Continue medical prevention without carotid reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The persistent absent cervical lumen represents established occlusion, not an ordinary severe stenosis to reopen through CEA.

answerChoices.label: Perform CEA with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Distal collateral opacification does not establish a patent cervical lumen suitable for routine endarterectomy.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Distal collateral opacification does not establish a patent cervical lumen suitable for routine endarterectomy.

answerChoices.label: Perform EC-IC bypass with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Bypass has not established a stroke-prevention advantage for this atherosclerotic occlusion indication.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bypass has not established a stroke-prevention advantage for this atherosclerotic occlusion indication.

questions.stem: Which assessment should inform Gordon Vale's airway planning for the right carotid operation?

answerChoices.label: Flexible laryngoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: An acceptable voice can coexist with an immobile fold near the midline. Directly establish current bilateral movement before exposing the opposite side to operative nerve risk.

answerChoices.label: Laryngeal electromyography
answerChoices.rationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.

answerChoices.label: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
answerChoices.rationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.

questions.explanation: The earlier examination demonstrated little left-fold movement with closure provided by the right side. Improved speech and cough do not establish return of left-fold movement. Laryngoscopy should document current bilateral mobility before the planned right CEA, because an existing left-sided deficit changes the consequences of right-sided laryngeal injury. Electromyography answers cause or prognosis after movement has been characterized. A positive examination still requires a patient-specific operative plan.

The episode resolved. Outside brain imaging shows no hemorrhage or established infarct. CTA measures left ICA stenosis at 76% and right ICA stenosis at 88% by NASCET, with normal distal caliber on both sides. She manages her daily activities independently and walks uphill without angina or dyspnea. Both lesions are accessible through a standard neck exposure, and the procedural team meets audited guideline risk criteria. Aspirin, atorvastatin and risk-factor treatment continue with every plan.

cases.presentation: Martin Bell, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after another resolved episode of left-arm weakness yesterday. Four weeks earlier, a similar event led to detection of atrial fibrillation. The initial team favored cardiac embolism and started warfarin. Recorded INRs since then are 2.4, 2.6 and 2.5, with the latest drawn during yesterday's assessment. Brain MRI shows two small recent right cortical infarcts without hemorrhage or edema. CTA shows ordinary 81% right ICA stenosis with a patent normal-caliber distal vessel and a low cervical lesion. He lives independently, walks without angina or dyspnea, and has no prior neck surgery or radiation. The procedural teams meet audited guideline risk criteria. Lipid treatment and the indicated AF prevention continue under the treating teams' perioperative protocol.

decisionNodes.stem: Which assessment should inform Gordon Vale's airway planning for the right carotid operation?

answerChoices.label: Flexible laryngoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: An acceptable voice can coexist with an immobile fold near the midline. Directly establish current bilateral movement before exposing the opposite side to operative nerve risk.

answerChoices.label: Laryngeal electromyography
answerChoices.rationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.

answerChoices.label: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
answerChoices.rationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.

decisionNodes.explanation: The earlier examination demonstrated little left-fold movement with closure provided by the right side. authoringCases.presentation: Jonah Price, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after resolved right arm weakness six days ago. Outside brain imaging shows no infarct or hemorrhage. Two expert reviews leave a left ICA duplex report below 50% and a CTA report above 70% in disagreement; calcific blooming obscures the CTA lumen. Renal function is at baseline. Aspirin, statin therapy and risk-factor treatment have begun.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: Node 1 resolves a genuine treatment-threshold discrepancy, rather than repeating a previously adequate study. Its feedback does not teach the NASCET denominator or sub-50% treatment rule tested by the new measurements in node 2. This case replaces the two repetitive hand-weakness supply rows without transferring their FSRS histories to different objectives.

nodes.objective: Use the distal normal ICA denominator to distinguish a mild symptomatic lesion from a misleading bulb-based percentage and select medical prevention.
nodes.currentUpdate: Angiography is complete. The original outside report called the left lesion '70%'. The right ICA has only a small plaque. Jonah has had no recurrent symptoms; medical prevention continues.

exhibit.caption: Constructed measurement record; fictional values, not a copied clinical image

nodes.task: Which left carotid treatment plan follows from Jonah Price's completed measurements?

choices.label: Continue medical prevention and carotid follow-up
choices.rationale: The NASCET reduction is 1 - 3/5 = 40%, below the ordinary symptomatic CEA threshold.
choices.temptation: Key: interprets the denominator before applying the intervention evidence.
choices.bestUnder: An ordinary mild symptomatic stenosis without recurrent events needing a separate evaluation.

choices.label: Arrange left carotid endarterectomy with medical prevention
choices.rationale: Using the estimated bulb gives the outside 70% figure but does not yield a NASCET 70% lesion.
choices.temptation: Trust the report label or use the large bulb denominator.
choices.bestUnder: A normal distal reference confirms ordinary severe ipsilateral symptomatic stenosis and operative context is appropriate.

choices.label: Arrange left carotid stenting with medical prevention
choices.rationale: A less invasive procedure does not create a revascularization indication for ordinary sub-50% disease.
choices.temptation: Use stenting to bypass uncertainty about CEA eligibility.
choices.bestUnder: Confirmed intervention-grade disease and a supported reason to favor stenting over CEA.

nodes.explanation: NASCET uses the normal distal ICA: 1 - 3.0/5.0 = 40%. The estimated bulb produces a different measurement, 1 - 3.0/10.0 = 70%. Apply the symptomatic treatment evidence to the NASCET result: routine CEA or CAS is not the plan for this mild lesion. Continue prevention and follow-up.
reasoning: Reject the supplied report label and calculate the narrowing with the normal distal denominator.
Apply the resulting mild symptomatic category to choose medical prevention rather than a procedure.
nodes.closestError: Select CEA from the outside 70% label without reconciling how it was measured.
nodes.decidingObservation: Residual lumen 3.0 mm, normal distal ICA 5.0 mm; the 10.0-mm reference is an estimated bulb.
nodes.deletionTest: Remove the measurements and the outside label favors surgery; remove the report label and the credible denominator trap weakens. The right-sided plaque prevents inventing a second operative target but does not teach the formula.
nodes.cueAttack: The table names raw measurement sites without identifying the keyed denominator. All choices are comparably scoped treatment plans with shared prevention. No measurement formula appears before answering. This is a clinical measurement-to-action item, not a statistics-exception node.
nodes.difficulty: Hard prediction: an authoritative but incompatible percentage competes with correctly reconstructed severity and intervention eligibility.

counterfactual.changedObservation: The narrowest lumen is 1.0 mm and the normal distal ICA remains 5.0 mm, without distal collapse; operative assessment is favorable.
counterfactual.result: An ordinary 80% NASCET symptomatic lesion supports CEA assessment.

authoringCases.presentation: The founder reviews Nora Lewis's outside hospital records in clinic. Nora is a 71-year-old woman admitted yesterday with persistent right arm and leg weakness and difficulty speaking. She needs help dressing and cannot walk independently. CTA shows left ICA stenosis of 84% with a patent distal lumen. CT shows infarction and edema involving about half the left MCA territory, without hemorrhage. The hospital stroke team is providing medical treatment.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: The game performs a record review, not hospital treatment. Node 2 is an explicitly later outside-record update after recovery; it does not assume that the learner's node-1 choice was executed. Its persistent occlusion changes the next decision despite resolution of the original timing barrier.

nodes.objective: Distinguish chronic ICA occlusion with distal collateral filling from a treatable severe residual stenosis after stroke recovery.
nodes.currentUpdate: Eight weeks later, Nora attends clinic independently after rehabilitation. Interval brain imaging shows the established infarct without edema or hemorrhage. CTA and expert duplex show no cervical left ICA lumen from its origin to the skull base on arterial or delayed imaging. The intracranial left ICA fills through communicating arteries. This appearance was also present on imaging four weeks earlier; she has had no new events.
nodes.task: Which long-term left carotid plan best fits Nora Lewis's current vascular findings?

choices.label: Continue medical prevention without carotid reconstruction
choices.rationale: The persistent absent cervical lumen represents established occlusion, not an ordinary severe stenosis to reopen through CEA.
choices.temptation: Key: separates recovery of the patient from recovery of an intervention target.
choices.bestUnder: Established stable atherosclerotic ICA occlusion.

choices.label: Perform CEA with continued medical prevention
choices.rationale: Distal collateral opacification does not establish a patent cervical lumen suitable for routine endarterectomy.
choices.temptation: Treat intracranial filling as proof that the cervical vessel is merely very tight.
choices.bestUnder: A patent cervical lumen with ordinary severe symptomatic stenosis and a favorable operative assessment.

choices.label: Perform EC-IC bypass with continued medical prevention
choices.rationale: Bypass has not established a stroke-prevention advantage for this atherosclerotic occlusion indication.
choices.temptation: Infer that restoring flow through a different route must improve stroke prevention.
choices.bestUnder: A separately established bypass indication outside atherosclerotic carotid prevention; this packet does not teach those other indications.

nodes.explanation: The serial absence of a cervical lumen on adequate arterial and delayed imaging establishes chronic occlusion. Communicating arteries explain intracranial filling without reopening the cervical ICA. Neurologic recovery removes the earlier timing barrier but does not create a CEA target. Continue medical prevention; routine EC-IC bypass is not recommended for atherosclerotic ICA occlusion.
reasoning: Interpret distal opacification through communicating arteries alongside a persistently absent cervical lumen.
Recognize that recovery from the infarct does not create an evidence-supported reconstruction for chronic occlusion.
nodes.closestError: Assume the old severe lesion can now undergo CEA because the patient recovered and the distal artery fills.
nodes.decidingObservation: Two examinations separated in time show no cervical lumen, including delayed phases, with a defined collateral route.
nodes.deletionTest: Remove delayed-phase and serial observations and near-occlusion or an acquisition problem remains possible. Delete the recovery update and old timing feedback could answer the item without interpreting the new anatomy.
nodes.cueAttack: Presentation does not call the vessel 'completely occluded'; adequate acquisition and actual extent are given. All plans include the same prevention background. Prior feedback discusses infarct timing and never teaches the occlusion/bypass answer.
nodes.difficulty: Hard prediction from reconciling distal filling with a persistently absent cervical lumen and rejecting an intuitively attractive bypass alternative.

counterfactual.changedObservation: CTA instead shows a continuous cervical lumen with ordinary 84% NASCET narrowing, normal distal caliber and no prohibitive operative finding.
counterfactual.result: The intervention target is restored and CEA assessment becomes appropriate after recovery.

authoringCases.presentation: Ruth Carter, a 70-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside assessment for a brief right-eye visual loss eight days ago. CTA shows a very tight right bulb lumen, a threadlike distal right cervical ICA, and delayed intracranial filling. The distal right ICA is smaller than both the opposite ICA and the right external carotid artery. Brain imaging shows no infarct. She has had no recurrence since starting medical prevention.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: A single decision is appropriate. Do not pair after a teaching explanation that already names the distal-collapse exception. Recurrent symptoms despite prevention are deliberately a separate unkeyed clinical hold, not a second node with an automatic operation key.

nodes.objective: Recognize the distal-collapse exception to routine severe symptomatic stenosis intervention.
nodes.task: Which right carotid plan best fits Ruth Carter's current evaluation?

choices.label: Continue medical prevention with neurovascular follow-up
choices.rationale: The distal-collapse pattern is not an ordinary percent-graded severe stenosis; ESVS does not recommend routine CEA or CAS in this nonrecurrent setting.
choices.temptation: Key: applies the narrow distal-collapse exception.
choices.bestUnder: The represented collapse-confirmed, nonrecurrent course.

choices.label: Perform early CEA with continued medical prevention
choices.rationale: The ordinary 70-99% symptomatic CEA benefit cannot simply be extended to distal-collapse near-occlusion.
choices.temptation: Translate a tiny bulb lumen directly into a routine high-percentage CEA indication.
choices.bestUnder: An ordinary severe symptomatic lesion with preserved distal caliber and favorable operative context.

choices.label: Perform early CAS with continued medical prevention
choices.rationale: Stenting does not automatically overcome the uncertain intervention benefit in distal-collapse near-occlusion.
choices.temptation: Assume endovascular access removes the evidence exception affecting CEA.
choices.bestUnder: An ordinary intervention-grade lesion with a supported reason for stenting; recurrent collapse disease first requires multidisciplinary review.

nodes.explanation: The distal artery has collapsed, so the usual percentage framework and intervention evidence do not transfer directly. With no recurrent symptoms on medical treatment, ESVS advises continued prevention rather than routine CEA or CAS. Evidence is limited, and ESO could not issue a clear recommendation; recurrent symptoms despite treatment require a separate multidisciplinary decision.
reasoning: Integrate the distal-caliber comparisons and delayed filling rather than infer severity from the tiny bulb lumen alone.
Apply the collapse-specific evidence boundary and current nonrecurrent course rather than the routine severe-stenosis operation rule.
nodes.closestError: Call the lesion 99% and select routine early revascularization from the ordinary severe-stenosis trials.
nodes.decidingObservation: Delayed filling and a distal ICA smaller than both the opposite ICA and ipsilateral ECA, with no recurrent symptoms after prevention begins.
nodes.deletionTest: Remove distal-caliber comparisons and early CEA becomes reasonable. Remove the treatment course and the conditional recurrent-symptom branch cannot be separated. Multiple supported anatomic relationships are supplied; a solitary small diameter would be inadequate.
nodes.cueAttack: Removed the expert's distal-collapse interpretation from the visible presentation. The learner must interpret the delayed filling and both caliber comparisons. All options retain identical prevention scope; none is a generic individualized plan. Guideline uncertainty remains explicit for Melissa rather than being hidden as a certainty claim.
nodes.difficulty: Hard prediction from knowing when severe-stenosis evidence does not apply. Key is limited to ESVS's nonrecurrent collapse setting and needs explicit clinician confirmation.

counterfactual.changedObservation: CTA shows ordinary 82% NASCET narrowing with preserved distal caliber, and the operative assessment is favorable.
counterfactual.result: The ordinary early symptomatic CEA pathway becomes appropriate.

authoringCases.presentation: Elena Ward, a 66-year-old woman, attends clinic six days after an episode in which she could not lift a cup with her right hand and repeatedly used incorrect names for familiar objects. The episode resolved. Outside brain imaging shows no hemorrhage or established infarct. CTA measures left ICA stenosis at 76% and right ICA stenosis at 88% by NASCET, with normal distal caliber on both sides. She manages her daily activities independently and walks uphill without angina or dyspnea. Both lesions are accessible through a standard neck exposure, and the procedural team meets audited guideline risk criteria. Aspirin, atorvastatin and risk-factor treatment continue with every plan.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: The returned imaging companion is parked. This standalone case supplies the episode and both arterial measurements together. The historical retinal-imaging case remains archived. The revised question uses the established bilateral symptom-attribution concept.

nodes.objective: Use hemispheric findings to prioritize the symptomatic carotid lesion before the larger opposite stenosis.
nodes.task: Which carotid plan should take priority at Elena Ward's visit six days after this episode?

choices.label: Left carotid endarterectomy assessment
choices.rationale: Right-arm dysfunction with a language disturbance directs attention to the left hemisphere. The left ordinary severe stenosis is the recent symptomatic target despite the larger right measurement.
choices.temptation: Key applies event localization before the intervention indication.
choices.bestUnder: The current focal episode and severe left lesion.

choices.label: Right carotid endarterectomy assessment
choices.rationale: The numerically tighter right lesion does not match the represented hemispheric findings.
choices.temptation: Treat the larger percentage as the procedure priority.
choices.bestUnder: The episode instead localizes to the right carotid territory and the right lesion remains appropriate for intervention assessment.

choices.label: Carotid surveillance with medical prevention
choices.rationale: A resolved recent focal event still makes its corresponding severe lesion symptomatic and warrants prompt intervention assessment.
choices.temptation: Classify the patient as asymptomatic because the examination has recovered.
choices.bestUnder: No carotid-territory event is established and prevention with surveillance is the selected plan after specialist assessment.

nodes.explanation: The right-hand loss of power and language disturbance localize the episode to the left hemisphere. The left ICA lesion is therefore the symptomatic severe lesion. Prioritize left CEA assessment while prevention continues. Appropriate symptomatic CEA is generally sought within 14 days. The right artery's larger percentage does not determine the symptomatic priority.
nodes.category: carotid treatment priorities at the current visit
reasoning: Localize the observed combination of unilateral motor loss and language disturbance before reading the two percentages as a treatment ranking.
Apply the recent symptomatic severe-lesion indication to the corresponding artery instead of the tighter opposite artery or recovered office examination.
nodes.closestError: Choose the 88% right lesion because its numerical severity distracts from the episode's territory.
nodes.decidingObservation: The right-hand and language findings accompany a severe left lesion while the right lesion is numerically larger.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the episode and neither lesion is established as the symptomatic priority. Delete the bilateral measurements and there is no competing numerically tighter target. Functional and neck observations establish the intervention context. The parked imaging explanation is absent from this standalone case.
nodes.cueAttack: Removed the procedure/timing intersection and the infarct-recovery contradiction. Both side-specific options use identical wording. The task identifies the dated visit and asks one priority decision. Current deficit recovery is retained because it is the surveillance temptation. No prior explanation supplies localization.
nodes.difficulty: Moderate-to-hard author prediction from attributing a resolved focal event and resisting the larger opposite stenosis. The target choice requires the supplied clinical findings.

counterfactual.changedObservation: The episode instead consists of left arm and leg weakness with a concordant right-hemisphere evaluation, and both stenoses are otherwise unchanged.
counterfactual.result: The right carotid lesion becomes the symptomatic procedural priority.

authoringCases.presentation: Martin Bell, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after another resolved episode of left-arm weakness yesterday. Four weeks earlier, a similar event led to detection of atrial fibrillation. The initial team favored cardiac embolism and started warfarin. Recorded INRs since then are 2.4, 2.6 and 2.5, with the latest drawn during yesterday's assessment. Brain MRI shows two small recent right cortical infarcts without hemorrhage or edema. CTA shows ordinary 81% right ICA stenosis with a patent normal-caliber distal vessel and a low cervical lesion. He lives independently, walks without angina or dyspnea, and has no prior neck surgery or radiation. The procedural teams meet audited guideline risk criteria. Lipid treatment and the indicated AF prevention continue under the treating teams' perioperative protocol.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: The renal-imaging companion is parked. This independent case supplies its own chronology, medication observations and current imaging. It changes the earlier age-only procedure comparison into reassessment of a recurrent territorial event during anticoagulation.

nodes.objective: Reassess recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation and select the appropriate carotid intervention route.
nodes.task: Which right carotid plan best fits Martin Bell's recurrent event and completed current assessment?

choices.label: Right CEA with continued vascular prevention
choices.rationale: The repeated right-territory events during in-range anticoagulation warrant addressing the ipsilateral severe carotid lesion. His age and accessible neck support CEA over the offered transfemoral route.
choices.temptation: Key reassesses the initially favored mechanism and then compares procedures.
choices.bestUnder: The represented recurrent territorial course with an operable ordinary severe lesion.

choices.label: Right transfemoral CAS with continued vascular prevention
choices.rationale: Revascularization is reasonable, but transfemoral CAS has a less favorable peri-procedural neurologic comparison in an otherwise operable patient older than 70.
choices.temptation: Correctly identify a carotid indication but equate endovascular treatment with lower procedural risk.
choices.bestUnder: CEA is unsuitable because of a consequential operative constraint and the stent anatomy and medical context are acceptable.

choices.label: Warfarin treatment with continued vascular prevention
choices.rationale: Maintaining AF prevention is necessary, but it does not resolve the new carotid decision after recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation.
choices.temptation: Allow documented AF to explain every later event without reassessing a competing cause.
choices.bestUnder: A completed neurovascular assessment supports a cardiac mechanism and does not establish a carotid intervention indication.

nodes.explanation: The serial INRs lie within the usual 2.0-3.0 warfarin range. Another left-arm event with right cortical lesions during that treatment requires reassessment of the severe right carotid disease. ESVS recommends carotid revascularization for recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation in this setting. Age 74 and the accessible neck favor CEA over transfemoral CAS. AF prevention still requires its own perioperative plan.
nodes.category: current carotid management plans after recurrent ischemia
reasoning: Interpret the INR chronology and the repeated focal territory as a reason to reassess the original cardiac attribution.
Apply the carotid recurrence recommendation and the older-patient procedural comparison to choose CEA while retaining the separate AF indication.
nodes.closestError: Continue the original anticoagulation-only carotid strategy because AF remains documented.
nodes.decidingObservation: A recurrent event in the territory of the severe right lesion occurs with contemporaneous in-range warfarin measurements.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the recurrent course or the anticoagulation observations and the ESVS recurrence recommendation is not established. Delete age and operative anatomy and the CEA-versus-CAS ranking becomes underspecified. Each imaging observation defines territory, infarct burden or the procedural target.
nodes.cueAttack: Removed the unbounded symptom-free delay and all repeated procedure/timing components. Three named management plans have comparable scope. The initial cardiac attribution is a historical chart decision that the learner must reassess. The presentation does not call the current event a carotid embolus.
nodes.difficulty: Hard author prediction from a genuine competing stroke mechanism plus a separate procedure-risk comparison. The exact ESVS recurrence recommendation is consensus based and requires clinical confirmation.

counterfactual.changedObservation: The same recurrent territorial events occur, but the cervical lesion and prior neck treatment make surgical exposure prohibitive while the vascular team establishes acceptable transfemoral stent anatomy.
counterfactual.result: Carotid revascularization remains indicated, with transfemoral CAS becoming the reasonable offered route when CEA is unsuitable.

authoringCases.presentation: The founder reviews Ada Reed's outside hospital record in clinic. Ada is a 71-year-old woman who received intravenous alteplase for right-arm weakness and a language deficit 48 hours ago. She now names objects, dresses and walks independently, and her examination has remained stable. MRI shows a single 9-by-6-mm left frontal diffusion-restricted focus without hemorrhage, edema or mass effect. CTA shows ordinary 84% left ICA stenosis with normal distal caliber and an accessible cervical lesion. No further event is recorded. The hospital continues medical prevention and will repeat neurologic and brain-imaging assessment before any carotid procedure.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: This new post-thrombolysis scenario is separate from Nora Lewis's exact passed chronic-occlusion context. The record supplies actual recovery and recent treatment. The earlier large-infarct version is archived under its original identity.

nodes.objective: Use recovery and infarct burden to distinguish a post-thrombolysis timing delay from a delay for disabling brain injury.
nodes.task: Which CEA timing plan best fits Ada Reed's recovery and treatment at this 48-hour hospital review?

choices.label: Plan CEA after six days from thrombolysis
choices.rationale: With a stable recovered examination and small infarct, the ESVS post-thrombolysis deferral is the relevant timing consideration. Eligibility must still be reassessed.
choices.temptation: Key distinguishes the treatment-related interval from an ongoing disability barrier.
choices.bestUnder: This stable small-infarct course after intravenous lysis, using the ESVS conditional recommendation.

choices.label: Plan CEA at the current 48-hour point
choices.rationale: Applying the usual early symptomatic pathway immediately overlooks the recent intravenous thrombolysis and its additional peri-procedural bleeding consideration.
choices.temptation: Read rapid functional recovery as sufficient to remove every reason for a short delay.
choices.bestUnder: A suitable stable patient has not received thrombolysis and the treating team selects expedited CEA after its completed assessment.

choices.label: Plan CEA after further functional recovery
choices.rationale: The current observations already show independent function and a small infarct. They do not establish the large disabling injury that would make an open-ended recovery-based delay the appropriate plan.
choices.temptation: Carry the large-stroke delay rule forward despite the observed current recovery and small tissue injury.
choices.bestUnder: The record instead shows a disabling deficit or a large edematous territorial infarct requiring improvement and reassessment.

nodes.explanation: Ada's current function and small nonhemorrhagic infarct support eventual carotid intervention assessment. Recent intravenous thrombolysis adds a separate timing consideration. ESVS advises considering a six-day deferral after lysis before CEA or CAS. For this stable course, use that short delay with the hospital's planned reassessment. It is a conditional recommendation, and it does not guarantee a procedure on a calendar date.
nodes.category: carotid procedure timing after intravenous thrombolysis
reasoning: Interpret current independent function and limited infarction as different from the original disabling large-infarct barrier.
Apply the separate post-thrombolysis timing consideration before selecting expedited CEA.
nodes.closestError: Treat the recovered examination as permission to apply the usual early-CEA schedule without the recent-lysis consideration.
nodes.decidingObservation: A stable independent examination and small infarct coexist with completion of intravenous thrombolysis only 48 hours earlier.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete thrombolysis and the current expedited option becomes reasonable. Replace the small infarct and independent function with a disabling large edematous infarct and recovery-based deferral governs. The source supports the six-day consideration directly.

authoringCases.sequenceReview: The returned perfusion companion is parked. This standalone operative record tests the timing and anesthesia-specific rescue distinction. It does not assume an imaging diagnosis or teach a later perfusion question.

nodes.task: Which immediate hospital rescue plan best fits Philip Grant's operative sequence?

choices.label: Re-explore the carotid reconstruction immediately
choices.rationale: The new neurologic change in the operated carotid territory appears after flow restoration during awake CEA. ESVS specifically recommends immediate re-exploration in this phase.
choices.temptation: Key interprets the observed phase before selecting the narrower intraoperative pathway.
choices.bestUnder: The represented awake clamp-release event.

choices.label: Obtain urgent brain CT and carotid CTA
choices.rationale: Urgent imaging is important for other peri-procedural deficits, but this record meets the specific awake clamp-release situation for immediate re-exploration.
choices.temptation: Apply the general imaging-first postoperative pathway without distinguishing the directly observed intraoperative onset.
choices.bestUnder: The patient initially recovers uneventfully after general anesthesia and develops a deficit later.

choices.label: Insert a temporary intraluminal carotid shunt
choices.rationale: He performed the tasks normally while the artery was clamped. A new problem after clamp removal is not the demonstrated clamp-related low-flow pattern that a shunt addresses.
choices.temptation: Attribute any intraoperative weakness to poor collateral flow during clamping.
choices.bestUnder: The awake deficit occurs during carotid clamping and resolves when flow is restored.

nodes.explanation: The tasks remain normal throughout clamping and fail immediately after flow restoration, with similar systemic pressures. Interpret this as the specific awake clamp-release neurologic event addressed by ESVS recommendation 92, which favors immediate carotid re-exploration. A deficit first recognized after an initially normal postoperative recovery follows an urgent brain/carotid imaging pathway. The table does not establish a definitive thrombus diagnosis.
nodes.category: immediate hospital rescue actions during carotid surgery
reasoning: Use preserved function during clamping and loss after release to distinguish the observed event from clamp hypoperfusion and a later postoperative event.
Apply the specific awake clamp-release rescue recommendation instead of the general imaging-first pathway or a shunt response.
nodes.closestError: Choose urgent CT/CTA automatically because it is appropriate for a later postoperative deficit.
nodes.decidingObservation: Normal awake speech and hand tasks during clamping change immediately after clamp removal.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the operative phase or anesthesia observations and the re-exploration-versus-imaging choice is underspecified. Reverse the during-clamp and after-release task responses and the shunt pathway becomes credible. Systemic pressures help exclude an unobserved major pressure drop.
nodes.cueAttack: Removed the named thrombus and the matching thrombectomy labels. Each option is an actionable hospital rescue plan. nodes.difficulty: Moderate-to-hard author prediction from recognizing the narrow awake intraoperative exception to a familiar general postoperative imaging rule. The rescue recommendation has one directly checked consensus guideline.

counterfactual.changedObservation: Philip undergoes general anesthesia, awakens with normal speech and strength, and develops the same deficits two hours later in recovery.
counterfactual.result: Urgent brain and carotid imaging becomes the appropriate offered first rescue step.

authoringCases.presentation: Gordon Vale, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic before planned right CEA for a recent left-arm event and ordinary 79% right ICA stenosis. After a previous left CEA, an ENT examination recorded the left vocal fold near the midline with little movement during breathing or phonation, while the right fold moved across to close the glottis. Following voice therapy, Gordon denies coughing with liquids. During the most recent audio-only follow-up, he read full sentences clearly and produced a strong cough.
authoringCases.sequenceReview: This standalone revision supplies the earlier observed movement and the later kind of reassessment. The learner must distinguish an improvement in voice from evidence of recovered mobility before the opposite neck operation.

nodes.objective: Distinguish an improved voice from established bilateral vocal-fold movement before contralateral CEA.
nodes.task: Which assessment should inform Gordon Vale's airway planning for the right carotid operation?

choices.label: Flexible laryngoscopy
choices.rationale: An acceptable voice can coexist with an immobile fold near the midline. Directly establish current bilateral movement before exposing the opposite side to operative nerve risk.
choices.temptation: Key distinguishes the observed function from what the current reassessment actually establishes.
choices.bestUnder: The represented prior opposite-sided movement abnormality with voice-only improvement.

choices.label: Laryngeal electromyography
choices.rationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.
choices.temptation: Treat a neural prognosis test as a substitute for observing present bilateral movement.
choices.bestUnder: Current laryngoscopy establishes persistent immobility and the clinical decision concerns its neural cause or recovery prognosis.

choices.label: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
choices.rationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.
choices.temptation: Infer that the original liquid-cough symptom makes swallowing mechanics the unresolved preoperative question.
choices.bestUnder: Current laryngoscopy documents normal bilateral movement but persistent aspiration symptoms remain relevant to the operative plan.

nodes.explanation: The earlier examination demonstrated little left-fold movement with closure provided by the right side. Improved speech and cough do not establish return of left-fold movement. Laryngoscopy should document current bilateral mobility before the planned right CEA, because an existing left-sided deficit changes the consequences of right-sided laryngeal injury. Electromyography answers cause or prognosis after movement has been characterized. A positive examination still requires a patient-specific operative plan.
reasoning: Interpret the older movement and closure observations alongside the later voice-only reassessment without equating acceptable phonation with recovered movement.
Apply that remaining uncertainty to the bilateral laryngeal risk of the planned opposite-side CEA and select direct current movement assessment.
nodes.closestError: Use the reassuring present voice as evidence that the opposite fold recovered, or substitute electromyographic prognosis for current mobility.
nodes.decidingObservation: The old fold remained near the midline while the other side closed the glottis, and the new assessment records voice and cough rather than endoscopic movement.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the old movement observations and the discrepancy between voice and mobility disappears. Delete the kind of current reassessment and repeat laryngoscopy may be redundant. Delete the planned opposite-side operation and the immediate bilateral airway-risk decision is lost.
nodes.cueAttack: Removed current breathy voice and liquid coughing as symptom-to-test shortcuts. Every choice is a named laryngeal or swallowing function investigation with its relevant estimate. The older observation is adequate for the uncertainty being tested. No absent action is named in the task, and no route ranking is supplied.
nodes.difficulty: Moderate author prediction from interpreting compensated phonation and the scope of a prior examination before selecting the investigation. All fairness issues identified by the first review are addressed, with the exact clinical version pending re-review.

counterfactual.changedObservation: A current endoscopic examination documents normal movement of both folds, but Gordon continues to cough and aspirate during swallowing.
counterfactual.result: Videofluoroscopy becomes the relevant remaining functional investigation.

review.title: Early procedure selection after transient monocular vision loss
clarityIssues: 'Early post-event period' leaves the operational timing vague, although the task anchors the patient at day six.
The delay option invokes recovery 'from infarction' when both presentation and update state there is no infarct.

cues.phrase: Left CEA during the early post-event period
cues.why: Convergence: CEA occurs in two choices and early timing occurs in two choices. The key alone combines both majority components, allowing a testwise selection without medical knowledge.

cues.phrase: No infarct or hemorrhage is present / after neurologic recovery from infarction
cues.why: A literal contradiction eliminates the delay option. No clinical interpretation is needed to recognize that the stated infarction does not exist.

fairness: Recent ipsilateral retinal symptoms, severe NASCET stenosis, preserved function and accessible neck anatomy support early CEA as the best offered plan; I identify no confident clinical inaccuracy in that direction.
Transfemoral CAS is a real competing procedure, but the third option is not a credible plan for this patient. The majority-component cue weakens even the remaining procedure comparison.

In sequence, the preceding explanation already localizes the retinal event. As a separately selected node with the presentation and update visible, the task is complete; it still lacks two consequential, unprompted steps.
High-yield topic: symptomatic stenosis, early treatment and CEA-versus-transfemoral-CAS selection. Exact current recommendations were not independently source-verified offline.
suggestions: Replace infarct-recovery delay with a genuinely plausible alternative at the same decision stage; do not remove the necessary negative brain imaging to make the existing distractor work.
Rebuild the option set so the key is not the intersection of repeated procedure and timing components. Do not add a fourth option solely for symmetry.
Use a supported patient-specific tradeoff to require interpretation before procedure selection. Name any necessary timing window only after source and clinician verification.

case.presentation: Elena Ward, a 66-year-old woman, attends clinic six days after an episode in which she could not lift a cup with her right hand and repeatedly used incorrect names for familiar objects. The episode resolved. Outside brain imaging shows no hemorrhage or established infarct. CTA measures left ICA stenosis at 76% and right ICA stenosis at 88% by NASCET, with normal distal caliber on both sides. She manages her daily activities independently and walks uphill without angina or dyspnea. Both lesions are accessible through a standard neck exposure, and the procedural team meets audited guideline risk criteria. Aspirin, atorvastatin and risk-factor treatment continue with every plan.

review.title: Procedure and timing selection in an older symptomatic patient
clarityIssues: 'After a prolonged symptom-free interval' is not a defined clinical plan and supplies no defensible reason for waiting.

cues.phrase: Right CEA in the early post-event period
cues.why: Convergence: 'Right CEA' occurs twice and 'in the early post-event period' occurs twice. Their intersection uniquely identifies the key without interpreting the patient.

cues.phrase: after a prolonged symptom-free interval
cues.why: The unbounded delay is a weak foil beside two actionable early plans. Its vague wording makes it easier to dismiss independently of the intended age-related procedure comparison.

fairness: Age 74, recent retinal symptoms, severe ordinary stenosis, functional independence and accessible anatomy support CEA over the offered transfemoral CAS plan. No confident clinical error identified; TCAR is appropriately not equated with transfemoral evidence.

The renal-imaging sequence is coherent: the update explicitly resolves the earlier acute renal dysfunction before this decision. Prior feedback already identifies the symptomatic retinal territory, so that cannot be counted again as an independent inference.
The age comparison is high-yield, but the current answer set permits a shortcut and offers no credible timing tradeoff. No difficulty credit is assigned for the undefined delay.
The task is complete with the shared presentation and current update. Exact contemporary recommendations were not independently verified offline.
suggestions: Replace the arbitrary wait with a credible patient-specific alternative and remove the majority-component intersection.
Require a genuine supported tradeoff in procedure or timing while keeping renal recovery and necessary stroke-burden information explicit.
Differentiate this variant's reasoning from the Elena item rather than repeating the same three-option pattern with an older age.

question.stem: Which right carotid plan best fits Martin Bell's recurrent event and completed current assessment?

answerChoices.label: Right CEA with continued vascular prevention
answerChoices.rationale: The repeated right-territory events during in-range anticoagulation warrant addressing the ipsilateral severe carotid lesion. His age and accessible neck support CEA over the offered transfemoral route.

answerChoices.label: Right transfemoral CAS with continued vascular prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Revascularization is reasonable, but transfemoral CAS has a less favorable peri-procedural neurologic comparison in an otherwise operable patient older than 70.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Revascularization is reasonable, but transfemoral CAS has a less favorable peri-procedural neurologic comparison in an otherwise operable patient older than 70.

answerChoices.label: Warfarin treatment with continued vascular prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Maintaining AF prevention is necessary, but it does not resolve the new carotid decision after recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Maintaining AF prevention is necessary, but it does not resolve the new carotid decision after recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation.

question.explanation: The serial INRs lie within the usual 2.0-3.0 warfarin range. Another left-arm event with right cortical lesions during that treatment requires reassessment of the severe right carotid disease. ESVS recommends carotid revascularization for recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation in this setting. Age 74 and the accessible neck favor CEA over transfemoral CAS. AF prevention still requires its own perioperative plan.

case.presentation: Martin Bell, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after another resolved episode of left-arm weakness yesterday. Four weeks earlier, a similar event led to detection of atrial fibrillation. The initial team favored cardiac embolism and started warfarin. Recorded INRs since then are 2.4, 2.6 and 2.5, with the latest drawn during yesterday's assessment. Brain MRI shows two small recent right cortical infarcts without hemorrhage or edema. CTA shows ordinary 81% right ICA stenosis with a patent normal-caliber distal vessel and a low cervical lesion. He lives independently, walks without angina or dyspnea, and has no prior neck surgery or radiation. The procedural teams meet audited guideline risk criteria. Lipid treatment and the indicated AF prevention continue under the treating teams' perioperative protocol.

question.stem: Which carotid intervention plan should the founder recommend when reviewing Nora Lewis's current hospital record?

answerChoices.label: Defer revascularization until neurologic improvement
answerChoices.rationale: Her disabling state and large infarct create a hemorrhagic-injury concern that supersedes routine early stenosis intervention.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with CEA during the acute neurologic decline
answerChoices.rationale: The early CEA benefit from stable nondisabling events does not justify surgery in this current large disabling infarct.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The early CEA benefit from stable nondisabling events does not justify surgery in this current large disabling infarct.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with CAS during the acute neurologic decline
answerChoices.rationale: Stenting does not remove the reperfusion and bleeding concern created by the injured brain.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Stenting does not remove the reperfusion and bleeding concern created by the injured brain.

question.explanation: Severe symptomatic stenosis is not sufficient to mandate early intervention. The functional deficit and infarct involving more than one-third of the MCA territory place Nora outside the routine early-CEA group. Defer carotid intervention until neurologic improvement and reassess in the treating hospital pathway.

case.presentation: The founder reviews Nora Lewis's outside hospital records in clinic. Nora is a 71-year-old woman admitted yesterday with persistent right arm and leg weakness and difficulty speaking. She needs help dressing and cannot walk independently. CTA shows left ICA stenosis of 84% with a patent distal lumen. CT shows infarction and edema involving about half the left MCA territory, without hemorrhage. The hospital stroke team is providing medical treatment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which long-term left carotid plan best fits Nora Lewis's current vascular findings?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Eight weeks later, Nora attends clinic independently after rehabilitation. Interval brain imaging shows the established infarct without edema or hemorrhage. CTA and expert duplex show no cervical left ICA lumen from its origin to the skull base on arterial or delayed imaging. The intracranial left ICA fills through communicating arteries. This appearance was also present on imaging four weeks earlier; she has had no new events.

answerChoices.label: Continue medical prevention without carotid reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The persistent absent cervical lumen represents established occlusion, not an ordinary severe stenosis to reopen through CEA.

answerChoices.label: Perform CEA with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Distal collateral opacification does not establish a patent cervical lumen suitable for routine endarterectomy.

answerChoices.label: Perform EC-IC bypass with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Bypass has not established a stroke-prevention advantage for this atherosclerotic occlusion indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: The serial absence of a cervical lumen on adequate arterial and delayed imaging establishes chronic occlusion. Communicating arteries explain intracranial filling without reopening the cervical ICA. Neurologic recovery removes the earlier timing barrier but does not create a CEA target. Continue medical prevention; routine EC-IC bypass is not recommended for atherosclerotic ICA occlusion.

review.title: Carotid timing after a large disabling infarct
clarityIssues: 'During the acute neurologic decline' appears only in the procedure options. The presentation describes persistent deficits since yesterday, not a documented ongoing decline.
'Until neurologic improvement' must not be read as an automatic promise of intervention once any improvement occurs; reassessment determines subsequent candidacy.

cues.phrase: Defer revascularization until neurologic improvement / during the acute neurologic decline
cues.why: Both distractors repeat a negatively loaded deterioration phrase; the key is the sole cautious option. This creates a wording shortcut independent of the infarct's measured extent.

fairness: A large infarct with edema and substantial disability is a valid reason not to apply routine early-CEA reasoning despite severe stenosis. I identify no confident error in deferring and reassessing.

The task directly supplies severe functional impairment and a large established infarct, then compares waiting with two poorly supported immediate procedures. The result is a high-yield safety-recognition item, not two difficult consequential decisions.
The later recovery and chronic-occlusion node follows coherently and tests a different barrier to intervention. This explanation does not give away that later vascular diagnosis.

The named patient, age and sex are present, but this is explicitly a retrospective clinic record review, not a patient currently presenting to the clinic. Do not depict the hospital procedures as clinic actions.
The explanation's exact infarct-extent criterion requires clinician/source verification; no network or fresh source validation was performed.
suggestions: Use the actual neurologic trajectory consistently; remove the invented decline wording from distractors.
Compare supported timing plans with a real competing consideration, preserving the infarct and disability observations needed for safety.
Alternatively retain it as an explicitly accepted safety-recognition exception, with easy difficulty and no two-step claim.
Keep hospital ownership explicit and make reassessment, rather than guaranteed later surgery, clear.

question.stem: Which CEA timing plan best fits Ada Reed's recovery and treatment at this 48-hour hospital review?

answerChoices.label: Plan CEA after six days from thrombolysis
answerChoices.rationale: With a stable recovered examination and small infarct, the ESVS post-thrombolysis deferral is the relevant timing consideration. Eligibility must still be reassessed.

answerChoices.label: Plan CEA at the current 48-hour point
answerChoices.rationale: Applying the usual early symptomatic pathway immediately overlooks the recent intravenous thrombolysis and its additional peri-procedural bleeding consideration.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Applying the usual early symptomatic pathway immediately overlooks the recent intravenous thrombolysis and its additional peri-procedural bleeding consideration.

answerChoices.label: Plan CEA after further functional recovery
answerChoices.rationale: The current observations already show independent function and a small infarct. They do not establish the large disabling injury that would make an open-ended recovery-based delay the appropriate plan.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The current observations already show independent function and a small infarct. They do not establish the large disabling injury that would make an open-ended recovery-based delay the appropriate plan.

question.explanation: Ada's current function and small nonhemorrhagic infarct support eventual carotid intervention assessment. Recent intravenous thrombolysis adds a separate timing consideration. ESVS advises considering a six-day deferral after lysis before CEA or CAS. For this stable course, use that short delay with the hospital's planned reassessment. It is a conditional recommendation, and it does not guarantee a procedure on a calendar date.

case.presentation: The founder reviews Ada Reed's outside hospital record in clinic. Ada is a 71-year-old woman who received intravenous alteplase for right-arm weakness and a language deficit 48 hours ago. She now names objects, dresses and walks independently, and her examination has remained stable. MRI shows a single 9-by-6-mm left frontal diffusion-restricted focus without hemorrhage, edema or mass effect. CTA shows ordinary 84% left ICA stenosis with normal distal caliber and an accessible cervical lesion. No further event is recorded. The hospital continues medical prevention and will repeat neurologic and brain-imaging assessment before any carotid procedure.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A later outside-record entry states that the carotid repair was revised and flow restored. On postoperative day four Philip develops severe left-sided headache and a focal seizure, which the hospital team treats. BP is 206/108 mmHg. MRI shows left hemispheric edema without restricted diffusion, with perfusion present throughout that tissue.

answerChoices.label: Titrate intravenous treatment to reduce blood pressure
answerChoices.rationale: The patent vessels and perfused edematous tissue with headache and seizure support a hyperperfusion complication requiring BP reduction.

answerChoices.label: Titrate intravenous vasopressors to raise blood pressure
answerChoices.rationale: Augmenting pressure would worsen the suspected perfusion-related injury rather than correct an occlusion.

answerChoices.label: Observe the blood pressure without intravenous treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent marked hypertension with this postoperative syndrome requires active reduction rather than untreated permissive hypertension.

decisionNodes.explanation: The later findings describe a different problem from the earlier thrombosis: patent vessels, headache, seizure and perfused edema without restricted diffusion support hyperperfusion. fairness: A new deficit after initial neurologic recovery, with imaging-confirmed fresh reconstruction thrombosis and a patent intracranial MCA, supports urgent hospital re-exploration. No confident clinical error identified in that direction.

Imaging appropriately precedes the proposed intervention in the supplied story. The issue is not that a diagnosis can never be supplied for management, but that this diagnosis leaves no difficult management tradeoff among these alternatives.

suggestions: Either obtain explicit acceptance as an easy emergency-recognition item or redesign the offered decisions around a supported, genuine post-CEA management distinction.

Keep the acute action in the treating hospital pathway and preserve the negative intracranial findings needed to choose safely.

question.stem: Which investigation should inform Gordon Vale's right carotid operative plan?

answerChoices.label: Flexible laryngoscopy during phonation
answerChoices.rationale: Prior opposite CEA with breathy voice and liquid cough raises concern for existing vocal-fold dysfunction; laryngoscopy establishes the airway-risk baseline.

answerChoices.label: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
answerChoices.rationale: Swallow testing can assess aspiration physiology but does not replace direct assessment of vocal-fold movement before contralateral CEA.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Swallow testing can assess aspiration physiology but does not replace direct assessment of vocal-fold movement before contralateral CEA.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced neck CT
answerChoices.rationale: An anatomic scan does not directly establish the vocal-fold movement required for this baseline risk assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An anatomic scan does not directly establish the vocal-fold movement required for this baseline risk assessment.

question.explanation: The old opposite-side operation, breathy voice and cough with liquids raise concern for pre-existing laryngeal dysfunction. Before right CEA, establish vocal-fold movement so bilateral dysfunction risk can inform the operative plan. A swallow study can answer a related functional question but does not substitute for laryngeal assessment. A positive finding does not automatically choose a particular revascularization procedure.

Right CEA is being planned.

review.title: Laryngeal assessment before opposite-side carotid surgery
fairness: Breathy voice and coughing with liquids after the previous opposite-side CEA make vocal-fold assessment a defensible best preoperative investigation. A swallow study addresses a related aspiration question but does not directly establish vocal-fold mobility; neck CT is not an equivalent dynamic examination.
No material knowledge-free wording, length, convergence or diagnosis-label cue identified. 'During phonation' describes the test, not an explanatory defense of the key.

The difficulty problem is the deletion test: even without the planned opposite-side CEA, persistent breathy voice after neck surgery supports laryngoscopy. The contralateral procedural risk is taught in the explanation but need not be interpreted to select the test; two consequential steps are not demonstrated.

This is high-yield preoperative cranial-nerve/airway safety content, but currently an easy symptom-to-test item. It is complete and coherent as a single node, with named patient, age, sex and clinic setting.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. A positive finding does not automatically rank CEA, transfemoral CAS or TCAR; the explanation appropriately avoids that leap. This offline review is not current-source verification.
suggestions: Preserve the preoperative safety concept, but make supplied prior examination or workup findings change which assessment is still required, with credible investigations at the same decision stage.
Alternatively seek explicit acceptance as an easy preoperative safety exercise; do not count recognition of hoarseness and recalling laryngoscopy as two consequential steps.
Do not manufacture a procedure-ranking sequel after confirmed vocal-fold palsy without a separately supported and clinician-reviewed patient-specific decision.

question.stem: Which assessment should inform Gordon Vale's airway planning for the right carotid operation?

answerChoices.label: Flexible laryngoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: An acceptable voice can coexist with an immobile fold near the midline. Directly establish current bilateral movement before exposing the opposite side to operative nerve risk.

answerChoices.label: Laryngeal electromyography
answerChoices.rationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Electromyography can investigate the cause and recovery prospects of an established movement abnormality. The immediate planning question is whether both folds currently move.

answerChoices.label: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
answerChoices.rationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Swallowing studies address aspiration physiology. They do not establish the current bilateral fold movement needed to assess the opposite-neck operative risk.

question.explanation: The earlier examination demonstrated little left-fold movement with closure provided by the right side. Improved speech and cough do not establish return of left-fold movement. Laryngoscopy should document current bilateral mobility before the planned right CEA, because an existing left-sided deficit changes the consequences of right-sided laryngeal injury. Electromyography answers cause or prognosis after movement has been characterized. A positive examination still requires a patient-specific operative plan.

case.presentation: Gordon Vale, a 72-year-old man, attends clinic before planned right CEA for a recent left-arm event and ordinary 79% right ICA stenosis. After a previous left CEA, an ENT examination recorded the left vocal fold near the midline with little movement during breathing or phonation, while the right fold moved across to close the glottis. Following voice therapy, Gordon denies coughing with liquids. During the most recent audio-only follow-up, he read full sentences clearly and produced a strong cough.
